blogs.title: Multiphasic Mayhem: Recognizing and Managing Recurrent Anaphylaxis
blogs.description: Defines biphasic vs multiphasic anaphylaxis, explores incidence variability and why it’s often missed, outlines known risk factors (delayed epinephrine, severe index reaction), compares true recurrence versus sustained symptoms, and offers a pragmatic algorithm—including repeat IM epinephrine and when to consider escalation—illustrated by a case with four episodes over 12 hours.

blogs.title: Epinephrine Shortfall: Why a ‘One‑Size‑Fits‑All’ Auto‑Injector Misses Heavy Patients
blogs.description: Analyzes weight‑based epinephrine dosing versus the fixed 0.3 mg auto‑injector most EDs stock, presents data linking underdosing to higher repeat‑dose rates and ICU transfer, provides guidance on calculating adult doses (>50 kg → 0.5 mg), how to safely draw up supplemental syringes, and recommendations for stocking both 0.3 mg and 0.5 mg devices in emergency settings.

blogs.title: Steroids Gone Stale: Updating the Anaphylaxis Playbook Without Corticosteroids
blogs.description: Summarizes historic rationale for systemic steroids in anaphylaxis, reviews the latest systematic reviews showing no reduction in biphasic reactions and potential harms (hyperglycaemia, longer admissions), clarifies current guideline positions, and proposes a decision tree that reserves steroids only for selected scenarios such as airway edema unresponsive to epinephrine.

blogs.title: Hidden Mast Cell Disease: When Systemic Mastocytosis Triggers Unusual Anaphylaxis
blogs.description: Explains how occult systemic mastocytosis amplifies mediator release leading to severe or multiphasic reactions, reviews tryptase kinetics and diagnostic thresholds, discusses limited WHO criteria and the role of bone‑marrow biopsy versus clinical suspicion, and offers a follow‑up pathway (hematology/allergy referral, prophylactic antihistamine regimens) illustrated by a patient with elevated baseline tryptase.

blogs.title: How Long Should You Wait? Tailoring Post‑Anaphylaxis Observation in the ED
blogs.description: Compares international monitoring recommendations (UK risk‑stratified tiers, NHG/WAO 4–6 h rule), examines evidence that ~50 % of biphasic events occur within 6–12 h, identifies clinical predictors warranting extended observation or ICU admission, and presents a bedside tool to decide between short stay unit, ward admission, or ICU based on severity markers such as repeat epinephrine doses.

blogs.title: Beyond Bolus Doses: When to Switch to Intravenous Epinephrine Infusion
blogs.description: Reviews indications for continuous IV epinephrine in refractory or multiphasic anaphylaxis—persistent hypotension despite ≥2 IM doses or rapidly recurring episodes—outlines infusion preparation (starting at 1 µg/min titrated to response), monitoring requirements (telemetry, arrhythmia surveillance), potential complications, and integrates a flowchart distinguishing when bolus therapy suffices versus when drip therapy is warranted.
